```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set( collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>" )
```

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library( governance )
library( dplyr )
library( ggplot2 )

theme_set( theme_minimal() )
```

This article walks through the path from raw 990 fields to governance scores
and explains each column the package adds. It uses the bundled `dat_example`,
a 5,000-organization sample of raw 2022 fields. In practice the data come from
`get_governance_data()`; see `vignette("download-data")`.

```{r}
data( "dat_example", package = "governance" )

set.seed( 57 )
rows        <- sample( nrow(dat_example), 1000 )
dat_example <- dat_example[ rows, ]
```

## Step 1: Code the practice items

`get_features()` returns the input with three groups of columns appended.

| Columns | What they are | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| 16 `GI_*` items | Recommended practices, 1 = present | the 2023 index (default) |
| 5 `RISK_*` indicators | Reported risk events or exposures, 1 = reported | not scored; reported alongside |
| 12 `P*_LINE_*` features | Features of the 2018 model | `get_scores( model = "legacy-2018" )` |

```{r}
features <- get_features( dat_example )
```

### Practice items

Each `GI_*` item records one practice. A blank answer is `NA`, not 0, and the
scoring model uses whichever items an organization answered.

| Item | Form 990 line | Practice |
|---|---|---|
| `GI_REVIEW_AUDIT` | XII-2a/2b, IV-12a/b | Financial statements compiled, reviewed or audited |
| `GI_AUDIT` | XII-2b, IV-12a/b | Financial statements audited by an independent accountant |
| `GI_AUDIT_CMTE` | XII-2c | A committee oversees the audit or review (0 if no review or audit) |
| `GI_ACCRUAL` | XII-1 | Accrual accounting |
| `GI_INDEP_MAJOR` | VI-1a/1b | At least half of voting members are independent |
| `GI_MINUTES_BOARD` | VI-8a | Board meetings documented |
| `GI_MINUTES_CMTE` | VI-8b | Committee meetings documented |
| `GI_990_BOARD` | VI-11a | Form 990 given to the board before filing |
| `GI_COI` | VI-12a | Written conflict-of-interest policy |
| `GI_COI_DISCLOSE` | VI-12b | Annual disclosure of interests (0 without a policy) |
| `GI_COI_MONITOR` | VI-12c | Policy monitored and enforced (0 without a policy) |
| `GI_WHISTLE` | VI-13 | Written whistleblower policy |
| `GI_RETENTION` | VI-14 | Written document retention and destruction policy |
| `GI_COMP_CEO` | VI-15a | Independent pay-setting process for the top executive |
| `GI_COMP_OTH` | VI-15b | Independent pay-setting process for other officers |
| `GI_990_WEB` | VI-18 | Form 990 posted on the organization's own website |

Practices differ a great deal in how common they are. Nearly every filer
documents board meetings; fewer than one in ten posts its 990 online.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
rates <-
  features |>
  summarise( across(starts_with("GI_"), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer( everything(), names_to = "item", values_to = "share" )

ggplot( rates, aes(x = share, y = reorder(item, share)) ) +
  geom_col( fill = "#1696d2" ) +
  scale_x_continuous( labels = scales::percent ) +
  labs( x = "Share of organizations reporting the practice", y = NULL )
```

### Risk indicators

The `RISK_*` columns record events that good governance is meant to manage:
business transactions with insiders (IV-28a/b/c), loans to insiders (IV-26),
family or business ties among officers (VI-2), use of a management company
(VI-3) and asset diversions (VI-5). They are not part of the index. They are
disclosures, not practices, and they rise with organization size, so they
correlate *positively* with good practice. Report them alongside the score.

```{r}
features |>
  summarise( across(starts_with("RISK_"), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer( everything(), names_to = "indicator", values_to = "share" ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
```

## Step 2: Calculate the scores

```{r}
scores <- get_scores( features )
```

`get_scores()` appends nine columns.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gov_score` | The governance index. 100 is the average 2023 filer and 15 points is one standard deviation; it runs from about 67 (no practices) to about 128 (all 16). |
| `gov_score_se` | Standard error of `gov_score`, in index points. |
| `gov_score_bf` | General factor of the bifactor measurement model (latent scale, 2023 mean 0). This was `gov_score` in version 0.1.0; see below. |
| `gov_s_finance` | Financial-assurance specific factor (audit, review, audit committee, accrual). |
| `gov_s_minutes` | Minutes specific factor (board and committee minutes). |
| `gov_s_policy` | Written-policies specific factor (conflict of interest, whistleblower, retention). **Not recommended**; see below. |
| `gov_s_comp` | Compensation specific factor (CEO and other-officer pay process). |
| `gov_count` | Number of the 16 practices reported (0--16). |
| `gov_n_items` | Number of the 16 items answered. |

### The index and the bifactor scores

`gov_score` comes from a graded response model in which each bundle of nested
practices is one ordinal item (financial assurance, conflict-of-interest
policy, minutes, pay-setting). With one dimension, reporting another practice
can only raise an organization's score. The `gov_score_bf` and `gov_s_*`
columns come from a bifactor model with a general factor and four specific
factors. That model describes how the items covary more closely, and its
general factor correlates .99 with the index, but its scores can *fall* when a
practice is added: in 2023 data, adding committee minutes lowered
`gov_score_bf` for most organizations that lacked them. Use `gov_score` as the
score. Use the bifactor columns only for the subscores described next.

The specific factors are *residuals*. They are uncorrelated with
`gov_score_bf`, and a positive value means the organization does more in that
area than its general level predicts. They are not standalone subscales: an
organization with a high `gov_s_finance` and a low `gov_score` is one that is
audited but has few other practices.

The specific factors are also much less reliable than the index. Among 2023
filers the empirical reliability of the scores is:

| Score | Reliability | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `gov_score` | .82 | Main score (the index). |
| `gov_s_finance` | .57 | The one subscore with substantial variance of its own; report it alongside `gov_score`. |
| `gov_s_comp` | .48 | Supplementary (two items). |
| `gov_s_minutes` | .41 | Supplementary (two items). |
| `gov_s_policy` | .29 | Do not use. |

**Do not use `gov_s_policy`.** The written-policy items are the core of the
general factor, so the policy factor has almost no variance of its own
(omega-hierarchical < .01). Its loadings only contrast the conflict-of-interest
items with the whistleblower and retention policies. The column is returned for
completeness. For simple domain-level measures, use the share of practices
adopted in each domain instead. Those shares are not residuals, so they move
with `gov_score`.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot( scores, aes(x = gov_score) ) +
  geom_histogram( bins = 30, fill = "#1696d2" ) +
  geom_vline( xintercept = 100, linetype = 2 ) +
  labs( x = "Governance index (100 = average 2023 filer)", y = "Organizations" )
```

### Score or count?

`gov_count` is a transparent alternative: the number of practices reported. It
correlates about .96 with `gov_score`. The model-based score adds three things:
practices are weighted by how much they reveal about governance, every score has
a standard error, and the scale is anchored to 2023 so it does not drift as
practices spread.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot( scores, aes(x = gov_count, y = gov_score) ) +
  geom_jitter( width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3 ) +
  labs( x = "Practices reported (gov_count)", y = "gov_score" )
```

The vertical spread at each count shows the weighting at work. Two organizations
that report eight practices can differ by 10 points or more, depending on
*which* eight. The written policies weigh most: in 2023 a whistleblower or
retention policy added about 10 to 12 points on average, a conflict-of-interest
item about 7, and most other practices 1 to 4.

### Precision

Scores are least precise at the ends of the scale, where few items
discriminate: the standard error is about 4 points in the middle of the 2023
distribution and about 10 points at the top and bottom. Treat differences
smaller than about two standard errors as noise, especially at the top and
bottom.

```{r}
scores |>
  mutate( quintile = ntile(gov_score, 5) ) |>
  group_by( quintile ) |>
  summarise( mean_score = mean(gov_score), mean_se = mean(gov_score_se) ) |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 1 )
```

### Missing answers

Rows with blank answers are still scored from the items they did answer; their
standard errors are larger. Rows that answered none of the 16 items get `NA`
scores.

```{r}
table( items_answered = scores$gov_n_items ) |>
  knitr::kable( col.names = c("Items answered", "Organizations") )
```

## Comparing organizations

Size is the strongest predictor of almost every practice, partly because
audits are required above state and federal thresholds. Compare organizations
of similar size, or adjust for size in a model. `vignette("overview")` shows the
size gradient across the whole sector.

To relate scores to size, sector or location, join them to the NCCS
[Business Master File](https://nccs.urban.org/nccs/catalogs/catalog-bmf.html)
on `ORG_EIN`. The snippet below is not run here because it downloads a large
file.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bmf_url <- paste0( "https://nccsdata.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/",
                   "bmf/unified/v1.2/UNIFIED_BMF_V1.2.csv" )

bmf     <- readr::read_csv( bmf_url )
bmf$EIN <- stringr::str_pad( gsub("\\D", "", bmf$EIN), 9, pad = "0" )

joined <- left_join( scores, bmf, by = c("ORG_EIN" = "EIN") )
```

## The legacy 2018 model

Earlier versions of the package scored organizations with a six-factor model
fit to 2018 data. It is kept for reproducing earlier work, but it has known
problems, including negative weights on several good practices. See
`vignette("legacy-2018-model")`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
legacy <- get_scores( features, model = "legacy-2018" )
```
